# Benchmarking RWE Against an RCT: Which Study Design and Analysis Choices Move the Estimate


NT


Nikhil Tiwari


Nov 23, 2026 ·


28 min read


Given the same database and the same question, five capable teams will return five numbers. When 29 teams analysed one dataset to answer one question, their odds ratios ran from 0.89 to 2.93 ([Silberzahn et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245917747646) ). Each number comes with a confidence interval, a methods section and a sound-looking rationale. Usually no one can say which is right, because the true effect is unknown. This post works through a case where a randomized trial has already answered the question, so every decision in the analysis can be benchmarked against it.


**TL;DR.** A randomized trial with a known answer (albumin does not change mortality in sepsis) was emulated in hospital records, and one analytic choice was changed at a time. The raw records showed about seven fewer deaths per hundred patients with albumin. If the trial is right, almost all of that was bias. Here is what each change did.


- **Time zero and the treatment window.** Widening the window in which a patient could count as treated, from 6 to 72 hours, moved the random-forest estimate steadily toward a benefit. With a wider window, treatment can depend on how a patient did in the first hours of follow-up, which opens the door to immortal time bias. A wider window also changes who enters the cohort. *What to check:* that follow-up starts at the same moment in both arms, and that the estimate holds with a shorter and a longer window.
- **Confounders.** Dropping the severity measures (labs, vitals, severity scores) moved the estimate about a quarter of the way back toward the false benefit, and keeping socio-demographics alone moved it halfway. Dropping the drug variables barely changed it. *What to check:* that the confounder list is drawn from a causal graph and holds nothing measured after treatment.
- **The models inside the estimator.** The same estimator, which combines a model of who gets albumin with a model of who dies, showed a large benefit with linear models and no effect with random forests. That was the biggest swing in the study. *What to check:* that the models were chosen by how well they predict patients they were not trained on, under a rule fixed in the analysis plan before any estimate is seen. Chosen this way, by a super learner, the estimate was −0.17 pp against the trial's −0.16 pp, though the trial's ±4.3 pp interval cannot rank it above random forests alone.


The question happens to be clinical, but the lessons are about the decisions an RWE or HEOR (health economics and outcomes research) lead signs off on: the protocol, the confounder list, the estimator, and the sensitivity analyses a regulator, health technology assessment (HTA) body or payer will ask for. Each section below covers one decision. It opens with how far that decision moved the estimate, explains how it can bias the answer, with the intuition before the maths, and closes with the questions to put to the study team. Readers who sign off on studies can follow the headings and those closing boxes; the five questions are collected inTable 9 .


## The study this post builds on


[Doutreligne and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.01605) , at Inria and MIT, wrote a step-by-step guide to causal analysis of electronic health records and tested it on a question with a known trial answer. They emulated ALBIOS, a randomized trial of albumin in sepsis, in MIMIC-IV, a public database of intensive care records. They varied the study design, the confounder set, the estimator and the models inside it one step at a time, and published[their code with every estimate](https://github.com/soda-inria/causal_ehr_mimic) . Their central finding is that every step matters about equally. Putting every step on one scale, this post finds one step that matters more than the rest.


This post starts from that study, extends it and examines each step in depth. Frekil reproduced the analysis from the published code: the same 18,421 adults with sepsis, the same 28-day deaths, and fresh estimates within 0.19 percentage points of the published ones. Three extensions are new here: who actually receives albumin in this hospital, a super learner that chooses the models inside the estimator by prediction accuracy alone, and every analytic choice on one scale. The estimates for the treatment windows, confounder sets, feature summaries, estimators and the linear and forest models come from[that study's published results](https://github.com/soda-inria/causal_ehr_mimic) , and all figures are redrawn from them.


## The vocabulary, one line each


Term What it means here


Risk difference (RD), pp 28-day mortality with albumin minus mortality without it, in percentage points (pp). −1 pp means one fewer death per hundred patients treated; negative numbers favour albumin.


Crude difference The RD with no adjustment at all: treated against untreated mortality as recorded.


Time zero The moment follow-up starts. In a trial it is randomization; in records, someone has to choose it.


Treatment window The hours after time zero within which albumin must start for a patient to count as treated: 24 h in the main analysis, 6 and 72 h as alternatives.


Confounder A variable that drives both who gets treated and who dies, such as illness severity.


Feature summary How a measurement taken many times before time zero, such as lactate, is reduced to one value per patient: first, last, median, or a combination.


Propensity score A patient's probability of receiving albumin, given their confounders.


Overlap (positivity) Every kind of patient had some real chance of either treatment, so propensity scores stay away from 0 and 1.


Estimator The recipe that turns adjusted data into one number: matching, weighting, outcome modelling, or a doubly robust mix of the last two.


IPW Inverse propensity weighting: reweights patients by their propensity score so the two arms look alike.


Doubly robust, AIPW An estimator that is right if either the propensity model or the outcome model is right. AIPW (augmented IPW) is the one used throughout this post.


Nuisance models The models fitted inside the estimator (the propensity model and the outcome model). Nobody reports them, but the answer depends on them.


Super learner A method that combines several candidate models, weighted by how well each predicts patients it was not trained on.


Vibration analysis Rerunning the study under every reasonable alternative choice and reporting how far the answer moves.


## The short version: the models inside the estimator moved the answer most


Before the details, here is the whole story in two charts. Figure 1 shows how far each decision moved the estimate: the spread, the highest minus the lowest estimate across that decision's options, with everything else held fixed. Spreads are in percentage points of the 28-day risk difference.


*Figure 1. How far each analytic choice moved the estimate. The models inside the estimator moved it 8.45 pp; each design choice moved it 1.55 to 3.06 pp. Spread across the options shown in Figure 2, AIPW with random forests unless stated. The estimator spread leaves out propensity score matching, which failed outright at +67.30 pp (Decision 3).*


Figure 2 shows every option behind those bars. Negative numbers favour albumin, and the trial puts the true value near zero. Each heading in the figure names one analytic choice, with everything else held fixed, and the rows under it are its options: each with its estimate, its 95% confidence interval and the value on the right. The grey spread beside each heading is the highest minus the lowest of those estimates. All rows use the doubly robust AIPW estimator with random forests inside it, except where the estimator or the model class is the thing being varied. The trial sits at the top for reference, and the dashed line marks no effect.


*Figure 2. Every option of every analytic choice, 28-day risk difference, AIPW with random forests unless stated. Super-learner rows are from this analysis (Decision 4); all other rows are published estimates. The 24 h, all-confounders and first + last rows share one specification but come from separate runs, which is why they read −0.38, −0.28 and −0.03; compare rows under the same heading, not across headings.*


Four things to take from them:


1. **The design choices each moved the answer by about 3 pp.** With random forests inside the estimator, the treatment window, the confounder set and the choice among IPW, outcome model, DML and AIPW each moved it by 2.8 to 3.1 pp. A gross error at any step breaks the estimate, and plausible choices at every step produce biases of the same order.
2. **The biggest lever is the least visible one.** Switching the models inside one estimator from linear to random forests moved the answer by 8.45 pp, more than any design choice. That decision often lives in a code repository, not in the protocol.
3. **How each patient's history is summarized mattered least.** The five feature summaries moved the answer by 1.55 pp, about half as much as the other design choices.
4. **A misfit model exaggerates every other choice.** With linear models inside the estimator, each design choice moved the answer one and a half to two and a half times as far (Table 7). Fix the models inside the estimator first, then vary the rest.


After the benchmark, the rest of the post walks through the analytic choices of Figure 2 in the order a study team makes the decisions.


## The benchmark: an RCT that already answered the question


The data are MIMIC-IV, the public intensive care database of Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston. The question is whether giving albumin on top of crystalloid fluids (salt solutions such as saline) in sepsis changes 28-day mortality. The benchmark trial is ALBIOS, a randomized trial in 100 Italian ICUs: 285 of 895 patients given albumin (31.8%) and 288 of 900 given crystalloids alone (32.0%) died by day 28 ([Caironi et al., NEJM 2014](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1305727) ). A meta-analysis of trials agrees, with an odds ratio of 0.93 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.08) ([Xu et al., Critical Care 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4284920/) ). Neither finds a difference in mortality.


That makes it a benchmark in the strict sense. When an analysis of the hospital records reports a benefit, its error can be measured against the trial, within the trial's own uncertainty.


The emulation cohort is 18,421 adults with sepsis on their first ICU stay. Follow-up starts at the first crystalloid, and a patient counts as treated if albumin starts within the next 24 hours. This is the "24 h cohort" of the main analysis; Decision 1 varies the window.

## Where the false benefit comes from: albumin goes to patients who rarely die


Start with what the crude −6.98 pp actually measures. If albumin does nothing, as the trials say, all of it is bias: the albumin patients were people who would have died less often anyway. The question to ask is how the albumin patients would have done without albumin, compared with the patients who never got it.


### Who gets albumin


The answer starts with where albumin is given. Table 2 tabulates albumin use by first ICU unit in the 24 h cohort. Use varied more than twentyfold. In the cardiac vascular ICU, mostly patients recovering from cardiac surgery, 52.5% received albumin and only 3.5% died by day 28. In the medical ICU, 7.6% received it and 25.6% died. About two-thirds of all albumin-treated patients were in the cardiac unit.

This is confounding by indication in plain view. Albumin is mostly a cardiac-surgery drug in this hospital, and cardiac-surgery patients rarely die. A crude comparison credits albumin with the low mortality of the unit where it is used. Use also changed over time: 13.1% of patients in 2008 to 2010 (n = 6,047), 23.2% in 2011 to 2013 (4,667), 24.7% in 2014 to 2016 (4,586) and 17.7% in 2017 to 2019 (3,121).


Two consequences carry through the rest of the post. ICU unit and calendar period are not among the 24 confounders the analysis adjusts for (listed under Decision 2). Severity scores must therefore absorb the whole difference between cardiac-surgery and medical patients, and any residual unit effect biases toward benefit. And in the coronary care and neurological units albumin is almost never given, so those patients have almost no treated counterparts to be compared with. That is a failure of overlap, also called positivity. Neither adjustment for unit nor overlap within units was tested here. For a study lead, the general point is that a tabulation of treatment by site, unit and period before any modelling is cheap, and it shows where confounding and poor overlap are likely to come from.

The bias term is that question in symbols: how the albumin patients would have done without albumin, against the patients who never got it. If albumin does nothing, the whole −6.98 pp is that term. Every step that follows is an attempt to drive it to zero.


### Why a better prediction model does not fix this


Consider a failure that tempts any team with good machine-learning tools. A gradient-boosting model was trained to predict 28-day mortality from the last measurements of the first 24 hours in the ICU. On held-out patients its area under the precision-recall curve was about 0.50, against 0.18 for a random classifier. When tested on only the measurements available before the first crystalloid (the emulation's time zero), it fell by about 10 points, to about 0.40 ([Doutreligne et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.01605) ). It had learned from information recorded after treatment began: shortcuts a prediction model can exploit that carry no causal information. A model can predict mortality very well and still be unable to say what albumin does, because prediction never has to separate the bias term from the effect.


## Decision 1. Time zero: wider treatment windows drift toward benefit


**In short.** Widening the window from 6 to 24 to 72 hours moved AIPW with random forests from +1.01 to −0.38 to −1.87 pp, toward a benefit the trial never found. Classifying treatment by what happens after time zero opens the door to immortal time bias, and each window also changes who enters the cohort.


The first defence against bias is to write down the randomized trial one would ideally run, then emulate it as closely as the data allow ([Hernán and Robins, 2016](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254) ). NICE's real-world evidence framework makes this its first design recommendation: "Design studies to emulate the preferred randomised controlled trial (target trial approach)" ([NICE RWE framework](https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9) ). Writing the table already exposes a gap: ALBIOS tested sustained albumin to a serum target, while the emulation contrasts any albumin in the first 24 hours. That is a different treatment strategy, and a reviewer will see it. The table also forces the team to say how treatment and outcome are found in the records, which matters because recording can depend on treatment. One example: albumin is costly, so a treated stay is more likely to carry a sepsis billing code, while among crystalloid-only stays only the severe ones may be coded.


### The mechanism: survival for free


In a trial, eligibility, assignment and the start of follow-up all happen at randomization. In records they can drift apart, and the gap creates bias. Suppose follow-up starts at ICU admission and a patient counts as treated if albumin is given at any point in the next 24 hours. To be counted as treated at hour 20, a patient has to be alive at hour 20. Those 20 hours are "immortal" for the treated arm. A patient who dies at hour 5 can only ever be counted as untreated.

A removes early deaths from the treated arm only, so the drug looks protective even if it does nothing. The wider the window, the more free survival the treated arm gets. NICE names the remedy in its framework: "Avoid time-related biases due to differences between patient eligibility criteria being met, treatment assignment, and start of follow up" ([NICE RWE framework](https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9) ). ICH M14 describes the same mechanism as person-time handled differently between arms "through either misclassification or exclusion" ([ICH M14](https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/ICH_M14_Step4_Final_Guideline_2025_0905.pdf) ). The standard fix is to start follow-up at the same moment in both arms, which a target trial forces the team to write down ([Hernán et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2016.04.014) ).


The emulation sets time zero at the first crystalloid in both arms and measures confounders before it. Albumin can still start later within the window, but the gap is short: a median of 6.7 hours (interquartile range 8.7 hours) against a median of 40 days to death. The cohort also requires every patient, treated or not, to stay in the ICU for the whole window. That removes the classic form of the bias: a patient who dies at hour 5 now leaves the study, instead of being counted as untreated. Two things remain. Treatment is still decided by what happens after time zero, so how a patient fares in the first hours can shape both whether they get albumin and whether they die. And because of the survival rule, the window decides who enters the study.


### What the window did: each wider window favoured albumin more


To test this, the analysis was rerun with 6, 24 and 72 hour windows (Figure 3). Even the crude difference, with no model at all, changed: −0.46 pp at 6 h, −6.98 pp at 24 h and −4.82 pp at 72 h. Each window is a different cohort with a different case mix. With random forests, AIPW (explained under Decision 3) went from +1.01 to −0.38 to −1.87 pp, and IPW from −2.49 to −2.89 to −4.08 pp. Both drift toward benefit as the window widens. Read as immortal time bias, this makes albumin look more effective the longer the window ([Doutreligne et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.01605) ). With every patient required to stay in the ICU through the window, part of the drift may instead be the change in who enters the cohort, and these runs cannot separate the two. Linear AIPW did not follow the pattern (−2.97, −8.56 and −6.36 pp), an early sign that the model class matters as much as the design.


*Figure 3. Estimates by treatment window. Each window defines a different cohort. 30 bootstrap replicates.*


The window is part of the question. When treatment can start at any time within it, the design-based fix is clone-censor-weighting. Each patient is copied into both arms at time zero, each copy is censored when it departs from its arm's strategy, and the analysis weights for that censoring ([Hernán et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2016.04.014) ). A version with baseline-only censoring weights was tried here and is not reported, because its diagnostics failed (see Limitations).


**Questions for the study team** Where does follow-up start in each arm, and could a patient be classified as treated using anything that happened after that moment?


**A good answer** A target trial table in which eligibility, assignment and time zero coincide in both arms, plus a rerun with a shorter and a longer window. If the crude difference moves between windows, the cohort moved, and the report should say so.


## Decision 2. Confounders: the severity measures carry the adjustment


**In short.** With all 24 confounders the estimate was −0.28 pp. Dropping the severity measures gave −2.11 pp, and socio-demographics alone gave −3.34 pp, against a crude −6.98 pp. Dropping the drug variables changed it by only 0.3 pp.

Only overlap can be checked in the data. Exchangeability rests on knowing why patients were treated, and it pulls against overlap: adding variables makes exchangeability more plausible, but variables that predict treatment and nothing else push propensity scores toward 0 or 1.


### Every variable has a role


Whether a variable belongs in the model depends on its causal role. A confounder causes both treatment and outcome, and adjusting for it removes bias. A mediator sits on the path from treatment to outcome, and adjusting for it removes part of the effect being estimated. A collider is caused by both, and adjusting for it creates an association that was not there. An instrument affects treatment only, so adjusting for it adds no protection and erodes overlap. An effect modifier changes the size of the effect and is what subgroup analyses look for.


The working rule: adjust for confounders and for nothing measured after treatment. The prediction model above failed because it had, in effect, adjusted for post-treatment information. The analysis takes 24 confounders from an expert causal graph: demographics and insurance, emergency admission, comorbidities, antibiotics, vasopressors, ventilation, renal replacement therapy, vital signs, lactate, urine output, weight, AKI stage, SOFA and SAPS II. NICE asks for the same discipline: "Identify potential confounders (including time-varying confounders) using a systematic approach and clearly articulate causal assumptions" ([NICE RWE framework](https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9) ). Even a careful list has timing traps. The first-day SOFA score, for example, might be a collider, because it can include values recorded after albumin.

### What the models did: linear AIPW missed by 8 points, forests matched the trial


With window, confounders and feature summary fixed, all five estimators were run with both model classes (Figure 6). The model class produced the largest shift in the study. AIPW gave −8.48 pp with linear models and −0.03 pp with random forests. DML gave −5.91 and −1.34 pp. Linear AIPW landed further from the trial than the crude difference, so the adjustment made the answer worse. IPW barely changed (−2.78 and −2.84 pp). ## Decision 5. Vibration analysis: report every reasonable alternative


**In short.** With forest models, each design choice moved the estimate by 1.55 to 3.06 pp; with linear models every range was wider. A misfit model exaggerates every other choice.


Several choices above had more than one reasonable option. Redoing the analysis under each and comparing the results gives error bars that go beyond a single statistical model. Following[Patel and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclinepi.2015.05.029) , this is called a vibration analysis. NICE asks for the same thing in its own terms: "Sensitivity analyses should reflect areas with the greatest concerns about risk of bias, or when data curation or analytical decisions were made despite notable uncertainty," including "differing time windows" and "alternative model specifications" ([NICE RWE framework](https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9) ). The windows, confounder sets, feature summaries, estimators and model classes above are the main experiments of that vibration analysis, and Figure 2 puts them side by side. For that spread to mean anything, the analysis itself has to be reproducible: the same code on the same data should give the same number. ## Limitations


Everything here comes from one dataset and one question. MIMIC-IV is a single US centre whose patients were less ill than those in ALBIOS, so a choice that worked here may not work elsewhere. The benchmark has its own uncertainty. The ALBIOS interval runs from −4.47 to 4.16 pp. It contains forest IPW (−2.84 pp) as well as forest AIPW (−0.03 pp) and the super learner (−0.17 pp), so agreement with the trial cannot rank those analyses. The emulated treatment strategy also differs from the trial's (Table 3). Agreement with the trial is a weak check and cannot rule out unmeasured confounding.


ICU unit and calendar period are not adjusted for, and severity enters only through recorded scores. An exploratory clone-censor-weighting analysis is not reported because its diagnostics failed. In that analysis, 390 treated-arm clones (the patient copies described under Decision 1) were still in follow-up at the end of the grace period, the hours allowed for albumin to start. Weighting left them an effective sample size of 110. The largest weight was 71, and weighting made balance worse on several covariates (age standardized mean difference −0.12 unweighted, −0.24 weighted). Not yet run: clone-censor-weighting with time-varying weights, overlap checks and trimming by ICU unit, the ALBIOS septic-shock subgroup as a second benchmark, multiple imputation, and estimators built on other principles (entropy balancing, covariate-balancing propensity scores, TMLE and BART).


## What this means for an RWE or HEOR lead: five questions before sign-off


Design, confounder choice and estimator choice matter about equally: ignoring any one gives an invalid estimate, while imperfect but plausible choices at each step lead to small biases of the same order. The extensions here agree on direction and add one thing: on one scale, the models inside the estimator mattered most.


For albumin itself, the best-specified analyses agree with the trials: no detectable average effect on 28-day mortality. The crude seven-point benefit is best explained by who received albumin, and a weak choice at any of several steps (socio-demographics alone: −3.34 pp; linear models: −8.48 pp) would have reported a benefit the trials never found.


For the people who sign off on RWE, the practical lesson is that the number in a report is only as good as the least-examined decision behind it. ICH M14 asks that sensitivity analyses vary "design, exposure definition, outcome definition, missing data, and limitations of the data source(s) selected, and analysis approach," pre-specified "in the protocol and or the SAP" ([ICH M14](https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/ICH_M14_Step4_Final_Guideline_2025_0905.pdf) ). NICE asks that results be presented "for adjusted and unadjusted analyses and for all subgroup and sensitivity and bias analyses" ([NICE RWE framework](https://www.nice.org.uk/corporate/ecd9) ). Before a number goes into a dossier, a submission or a publication, five questions are worth asking:

- **Confounders from a cited causal graph.** Each edge in the graph carries a source, the adjustment set is read off it, and covariates are never selected by data-driven methods.
- **A statistical analysis plan locked before data.** The SAP names the primary estimator and specifies every model inside it. When a model is fitted by machine learning, the SAP states the algorithm, how its tuning parameters are chosen and the metrics that validate it. Cross-fitted doubly robust estimators are the supported route to valid intervals with such models. Balance and overlap are checked before any outcome is examined, with a pre-specified response if they fail.
- **Sensitivity analyses ranked by threat.** The plan ranks the threats most likely to make this study's answer wrong, such as unmeasured confounding, misclassification, censoring or model specification. - **Control outcomes alongside the main question.** Negative and positive control outcomes run on the same cohort, so the design's bias is measured instead of assumed (see[negative controls and empirical calibration](https://www.frekil.com/blog/empirical-calibration-negative-controls-rwe/) ).
- **Code that can be opened.** The AI writes the code, never the result. Every number comes from code that can be read and rerun.
